name: Brussels Airport
before:
Belgium's main airport, at Zaventem 12 km north east of Brussels, and home base for Brussels Airlines and TUI fly Belgium. It handled more than 26 million passengers in 2019, twenty sixth busiest in Europe.

Everything works under one roof, on stacked levels. The railway station is below ground, buses and taxis at street level, arrivals on level 2 and departures on level 3, with two piers, A and B, running off the top two levels.

The connection between those piers used to be the weak point. Pier A was reached by a 400 metre tunnel under the apron and each pier had its own security zone, so moving between them meant clearing security again and the airport worked in practice as two terminals. That changed in March 2015 when the Connector opened, an above ground building joining the two.

Pier A handles Schengen flights, plus Brussels Airlines services to Africa and to New York, which is why some of its gates were renumbered from A to T.

The departures hall was severely damaged by two bombings in March 2016 and the airport was closed until 3 April. It has since returned to full operation, reaching a record 96,000 passengers in one day in August 2019.
after:
Belgium's main airport, at Zaventem 12 km north east of Brussels. It handled 24.4 million passengers in 2025, and it is the hub for Brussels Airlines, Belgium's home carrier, as well as a base for TUI fly Belgium.

Since March 2015 an above-ground building, the Connector, has linked the terminal with Pier A. Before that, passengers reached Pier A through a tunnel under the apron.

The departure hall was hit by suicide bombings on 22 March 2016, and the airport stayed closed to passenger flights until 3 April.
